PLAINTIFE’S REPLY IN SUPPORT OF HIS MOTION FOR LEAVE
TO SERVE LIMITED DISCOVERY UNDER RULE 26(d)(1)

INTRODUCTION

NCMEC moves to dismiss on the ground that its statements are true. It then opposes the
three interrogatories that would test that ground. NCMEC cannot both assert the truth of the records
it holds and forbid Plaintiff from learning what those records say. Three questions decide the

Motion.

ARGUMENT
I. Why Do These Three Answers Matter?

Because NCMEC moves to dismiss on the ground that “[t]he Statements are True, and Thus
Not Actionable,” and because NCMEC’s own Motion does not say what the underlying reports

identify. That omission controls this dispute.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 36 Filed 08/27/26 Page 2 of 6 PagelD# 380

NCMEC states that the CyberTipline linkage could concern Plaintiff, could concern “a
person with the same name,” or could concern an email address. Those are three different facts.
The April 22 letters join Plaintiff’s legal name, the name Plaintiff uses, and Plaintiff’s email
identifier with the connector “and/or.” The letters do not say which identifier appeared in either
report as NCMEC originally received it.

The three interrogatories ask that one question.

The question is not speculative. Plaintiff has declared, under penalty of perjury, that he
never used “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to identify or operate a Meta account. Plaintiff declared that he
used “Jay Ballentine.” Plaintiff declared that his full legal name appeared in the April 9 materials
because it was his legal and litigation name. Interrogatory No. 1 asks whether “Marvelle J.
Ballentine” appeared in either CyberTipline report as NCMEC originally received it, or whether
that name entered only through Plaintiff’s later litigation materials.

Plaintiff does not seek discovery to learn whether he has a claim. Plaintiff seeks three
source-level facts. Those facts test a truth defense NCMEC has already asked the Court to decide.

II. Why Are the Answers Needed Now?

Because NCMEC asks the Court to decide the truth of its statements now, and truth cannot
be decided against Plaintiff without the records these answers identify.

Truth is an affirmative defense. It supports dismissal at the pleading stage only when it
appears on the face of the Complaint. It does not appear here. It depends on the contents of two
CyberTipline reports that exist nowhere in the record and that only NCMEC holds. NCMEC
confirms this. NCMEC states that Plaintiff “simply cannot possibly know” what those reports
contain, and asks the Court to dismiss on that basis. NCMEC’s own Motion supplies three different

possibilities in answer to that question. It states the linkage could concern Plaintiff, a person of the

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 36 Filed 08/27/26 Page 3 of 6 PagelD# 381

same name, or an email address. A truth defense cannot be granted while the defendant’s own
submission leaves the identifying fact in three versions, only one of which makes the
representation true as to Plaintiff. The three answers resolve which version the source records
contain.

That produces two paths, and both require these answers before any ruling.

If the Court decides truth on the pleadings, the defense fails now. The defense does not
appear on the face of the Complaint. The discovery is not premature.

If the Court instead weighs the reports NCMEC invokes, Rule 12(d) converts the Motion to
one for summary judgment, and Rule 56(d) entitles Plaintiff to the limited discovery needed to
respond. These three answers are that discovery, and no more.

The prejudice is definite. Without these answers, a dispositive ruling would decide the truth
of NCMEC’s statements against Plaintiff before Plaintiff could obtain the records on which truth
depends. That is the unusual circumstance Rule 26(d)(1) addresses. The answers are needed now
because the ruling NCMEC seeks comes now.

III. Why Is This Particular Discovery Appropriate?

Because the discovery is limited to the information NCMEC has made material.

The Motion seeks three interrogatories about two identified records. Each interrogatory
permits one of three answers: “Yes,” “No,” or “Unable to determine after reasonable inquiry.” The
interrogatories seek no reports. They seek no narratives, no provider identities, no victim
information, no dates, no report numbers, and no metadata. They seek no general discovery. They
exclude Plaintiff-supplied information, court filings, and public sources. They exclude information

obtained or added after NCMEC originally received the reports.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 36 Filed 08/27/26 Page 4 of 6 PagelD# 382

NCMEC identifies no burden. NCMEC identifies no expense. NCMEC identifies no
disclosure of protected report content that the three answers would cause. NCMEC’s objection is
categorical instead: no discovery before Rule 26(f), “regardless of how limited” the request.

Rule 26(d)(1) permits the Court to authorize discovery before the conference. The
discovery here is three closed answers about two records. NCMEC made those records material to
a defense it asks the Court to decide now.

The Motion should be granted.
